newsitem.title: USA: Drug cocktail can cut AIDS bloodstream level - study.
newsitem.headline: Drug cocktail can cut AIDS bloodstream level - study.

text.p: When patients with advanced AIDS took a combination or "cocktail" of three drugs, the AIDS virus was reduced to undetectable levels in the bloodstream of many, according to a new study.

In a study of 320 patients with advanced AIDS using three AIDS drugs -- Merck and Co's protease inhibitor Crixivan, Glaxo Wellcome plc's AZT, or zidovudine, and 3TC -- 65 percent had the AIDS virus in the bloodstream reduced to undetectable levels after 24 weeks, Merck said.
BioChem Pharma Inc manufactures 3TC, or lamivudine. Crixivan is also known as indinavir.

The study was conducted by independent researchers and sponsored by Merck, the company said. It was presented at the fourth conference on retroviruses and opportunistic infections in Washington, DC, it said.

Research found sustained supression of the AIDs virus for up to 68 weeks in 86 percent of patients whose virus in the bloodstream had already been lowered below detection by triple therapy, or the combined therapy of three drugs, Merck said.

Patients in the trial also had significant reductions, although not to undetectable levels, in virus levels in lymph nodes, which could harbor the AIDS virus even when it was no longer detectable in the bloodstream, the company said.

"For so many patients with high viral loads and very low CD4 cell counts to have their virus lowered to undetectable is remarkable, demonstrating that even people with very advanced disease can benefit dramatically from triple therapy with indinavir, zidovudine and lamivudine," Dr. Martin Hirsch, professor of medicine at Harvard Medical School and the study's lead investigator, said.
CD4 cells are key cells which HIV destroys, undermining the immune system. A low count of these cells would indicate advanced AIDS.
